label: Go Backend (Intermediate)
blurb: Go backend interview prep for 2–6 YOE: goroutines, channels, interfaces, generics, gRPC, database/sql, GORM, Gin, Kafka, system design, security, and behavioral questions that come up at cloud-native and SRE-focused companies.
audience: 2–6 YOE Go developers, engineers moving from another backend language, cloud-native / SRE candidates

modules.title: Core Go & Types
modules.intro: Core Go interview questions are the baseline every interviewer uses to calibrate a Go backend candidate. This module covers the type system from first principles — the distinction between value types (int, struct, array) and reference types (slice, map, channel, pointer), zero values and why Go initialises every variable to a predictable state, pointer semantics including when to use *T vs T for function parameters and receiver methods, constants and the iota counter for enums, type assertions and type switches for working with interface values, and the named return value pattern along with its trade-offs. The blank identifier _ and its uses (discarding values, ensuring interface satisfaction at compile time) appear in real code and in interviews. Every answer explains what the interviewer is actually testing — whether you know that passing a struct by value copies the whole struct and passing a pointer shares state — not just the syntax.

modules.title: Interfaces, Embedding & Composition
modules.intro: Go interfaces are the most interview-tested aspect of the type system, and they work unlike interfaces in Java or Python. This module covers implicit interface satisfaction (you never declare 'implements'), interface composition (embedding one interface in another), struct embedding as Go's answer to inheritance (promoted fields and methods, the method set rules), the empty interface interface{} and its modern alias any — when to use it and when it signals a design smell. The Stringer and error interfaces are the two every Go developer implements, and both are covered in depth. The famous interface nil pitfall (a non-nil interface value wrapping a nil pointer) trips up experienced developers in interviews and in production; it is explained with a runnable example and the canonical fix. Every answer distinguishes Go composition from classical inheritance.

modules.title: Generics in Go
modules.intro: Generics arrived in Go 1.18 and changed how you write reusable library code. This module covers type parameters (the square-bracket syntax func Map[T, U any](s []T, f func(T) U) []U), type constraints (interface-based constraints, the comparable built-in for maps and ==, the golang.org/x/exp/constraints package for Ordered), type inference so callers rarely need to spell out the type argument, and the critical design question that comes up in every generics interview: when do generics actually help and when does an interface do the job better? Go generics deliberately do not support operator overloading or runtime dispatch — these omissions are intentional and interviewers probe whether you understand the trade-offs. Every answer includes a real use case from production code (generic Result[T] type, Map/Filter/Reduce pipeline) and the anti-pattern it replaces.

modules.title: Error Handling in Go
modules.intro: Go error handling is idiomatic, explicit, and deliberately different from try/catch — and every interviewer will probe whether you understand why. This module covers the error interface (the simplest interface in Go: one method, Error() string), the idiomatic pattern of returning (value, error) from functions, wrapping errors with fmt.Errorf('...: %w', err) to preserve the error chain, errors.Is for identity checks and errors.As for type-based extraction, sentinel errors (var ErrNotFound = errors.New) for known expected conditions, and custom error types that carry additional context. The panic/recover mechanism is covered with the rule that separates idiomatic Go from Go written by Java developers: panic is for programmer errors and unrecoverable states; expected error conditions always use the error return value. Every answer includes the trade-off between verbosity and explicitness that makes Go error handling polarising.

modules.title: Go Runtime, GC & Memory
modules.intro: Go runtime questions come up at senior and staff-level interviews, especially at companies running Go services at scale. This module covers escape analysis (the compiler decides stack vs heap at compile time; variables that 'escape' are heap-allocated and GC'd — use go build -gcflags='-m' to see decisions), the concurrent tri-color mark-sweep garbage collector (mark phase, sweep phase, write barrier, why Go's GC pauses are sub-millisecond by design), GOGC and GOMEMLIMIT for tuning, pprof for CPU profiling (goroutine blocking, function call stacks) and memory profiling (heap allocations, allocation sites), the race detector (-race flag and what it catches), GOMAXPROCS and the Go scheduler's M:P:G model (OS threads, logical processors, goroutines), and benchmarking with testing.B. These questions separate Go developers who understand the runtime from those who just write goroutines.

modules.title: Goroutines & Channels
modules.intro: Goroutines and channels are the reason Go is Go — the combination that makes Go attractive for cloud-native, network services, and high-concurrency backends. This module covers goroutine creation (go func(){}(), the green-thread model, why goroutines start at 2 KB vs OS threads at 1–8 MB), channel semantics (sends block when full, receives block when empty, buffered channels decouple sender from receiver), directional channels (chan<- for send-only, <-chan for receive-only — used in function signatures to communicate intent), ranging over a channel until it's closed, the close semantics (close signals no more values; receiving from a closed channel returns the zero value), goroutine leak patterns (the most common production bug in Go), and the fan-out/fan-in concurrency pattern for distributing work across goroutines and collecting results. Every answer includes a code example the interviewer expects to see.

modules.title: select, Context & Cancellation
modules.intro: The select statement and context package are the two tools that make Go concurrency production-grade. This module covers the select statement as the multiplexer for channel operations (how to wait on multiple channels, how the default case makes a non-blocking receive, the random selection when multiple channels are ready), context.Background and context.TODO for root contexts, context.WithCancel to propagate cancellation signals down a call chain, context.WithTimeout and context.WithDeadline for deadline-driven cancellation, context.WithValue for request-scoped metadata (and the type-key pattern to avoid collisions), and how to wire context through an entire Go service (HTTP handler → service layer → repository → database query). The classic interview question is 'what happens if you call cancel() twice?' and 'why does context.WithValue use interface{} for keys?'. Every answer shows the full cancellation propagation pattern interviewers look for in production-grade Go code.

modules.title: sync Package (Mutex, WaitGroup, Once, Pool)
modules.intro: The sync package provides low-level synchronisation primitives for when channels are the wrong tool. This module covers sync.Mutex and sync.RWMutex (the classic producer/consumer and read-heavy cache patterns, the 'copy lock' pitfall), sync.WaitGroup for waiting on a group of goroutines to finish (Add before goroutine, Done in goroutine, Wait in caller — the off-by-one error that causes panics), sync.Once for lazy singleton initialisation (thread-safe exactly-once execution, why it's preferred over init()), sync.Pool for reducing GC pressure in high-throughput code (the HTTP handler that pools byte.Buffer allocations), sync.Map for concurrent maps without external locking (trade-offs vs map + Mutex), and the sync/atomic package for lock-free integer operations. The interview litmus test is 'when would you use a Mutex instead of a channel?' — this module answers that question precisely.

modules.title: Advanced Concurrency Patterns
modules.intro: Advanced Go concurrency patterns are what separate Go developers who write working concurrent code from those who write safe, maintainable, production-grade concurrent code. This module covers the worker pool pattern (a fixed number of goroutines processing a job channel — how to size the pool, how to drain it cleanly on shutdown), the pipeline pattern (stages connected by channels, how to propagate cancellation through the pipeline), the semaphore pattern for capping concurrency (buffered channel as semaphore, the golang.org/x/sync/semaphore package), golang.org/x/sync/errgroup for running a group of goroutines and collecting the first error with cancellation, the singleflight pattern (deduplicating concurrent identical requests — critical for cache stampede prevention), and the done-channel pattern for signalling goroutine shutdown. Every pattern is presented as a problem first: 'you have 10,000 tasks and want to process with max 50 concurrent workers — how do you implement that safely in Go?'

modules.title: net/http Standard Library
modules.intro: Go's net/http standard library is powerful enough to run production services without a framework — and interviewers at companies like Google, Stripe, and Cloudflare often test whether you know it deeply. This module covers the http.Handler interface and http.HandlerFunc type (the adapter pattern that makes any function an HTTP handler), http.ServeMux routing (the 1.22+ enhanced routing with methods and wildcards vs third-party routers), the middleware pattern using handler wrapping (logging, authentication, request ID injection), the request lifecycle (how to read body, query params, headers safely), the http.Client and its critical configuration (Transport, connection pooling, idle connection timeout — the production pitfall of creating a new client per request), and how to set read/write/idle timeouts on the server to prevent goroutine leaks from slow clients. These topics come up in every Go web interview as a baseline before discussing frameworks.

modules.title: Gin Web Framework
modules.intro: Gin is the most widely used Go web framework and the one most likely to appear in a Go backend job description. This module covers Gin's router (httprouter under the hood, route groups for versioning, named parameters and wildcards), the gin.Context object (the central type wrapping request and response — how it differs from the stdlib approach), middleware using gin.HandlerFunc and c.Next() (the abort pattern for short-circuiting authentication failures), binding request bodies to structs with ShouldBindJSON, ShouldBindQuery, ShouldBindForm (and the validation tags from go-playground/validator), Gin's error-handling model (c.Error accumulates errors; custom recovery middleware), and how to test Gin handlers with httptest.NewRecorder. The critical comparison is Gin vs net/http stdlib: when does Gin's convenience justify the dependency?

modules.title: Echo & Chi
modules.intro: Echo and Chi are the two most common Go web framework alternatives to Gin. This module covers Echo's design philosophy (the echo.Context interface centralising request/response, middleware as echo.MiddlewareFunc, built-in binder supporting JSON/XML/form/query, echo.Validator interface for custom validation), and Chi's different philosophy (Chi is a router that speaks net/http natively — every handler is an http.Handler, no custom context type, every piece of middleware in the ecosystem works without adapters). The framework comparison questions are what interviewers reach for: 'why would you choose Chi over Gin?' (answer: Chi handlers are 100% compatible with the stdlib middleware ecosystem; Gin has a custom Context type that breaks compatibility), 'why would you choose Echo over Gin?' (answer: Echo's interface-based binder is more flexible; middleware composition is cleaner). Every answer includes real production trade-off reasoning.

modules.title: Fiber
modules.intro: Fiber is built on fasthttp (not net/http) and is popular in performance-critical Go services and among developers coming from Node.js Express. This module covers Fiber's architecture (fasthttp's zero-allocation approach to request handling — why it's faster on benchmarks but breaks stdlib middleware compatibility), Fiber's router and ctx object (Express-inspired API: c.Body(), c.JSON(), c.Status()), Fiber middleware (CORS, rate limiting, logger, recover — the built-in set vs writing your own), and the critical interview question that frames every Fiber discussion: 'Fiber is faster than Gin on benchmarks — should you always choose it?' The answer is nuanced (stdlib compatibility matters for the Go ecosystem, fasthttp's context is not goroutine-safe across async boundaries, most production services are not bottlenecked on HTTP framework overhead) and interviewers are testing that nuance.

modules.title: database/sql & sqlx
modules.intro: The database/sql package is Go's built-in database abstraction layer, and sqlx extends it without abstracting it away. This module covers the connection pool (sql.Open returns a pool, not a connection; SetMaxOpenConns, SetMaxIdleConns, SetConnMaxLifetime — the settings that prevent connection exhaustion under load), the query API (db.Query for multiple rows, db.QueryRow for one, db.Exec for mutations), correct rows.Scan and rows.Close patterns (forgetting defer rows.Close() leaks connections), prepared statements (Stmt, the production trade-off vs query overhead), transactions with db.Begin / tx.Rollback / tx.Commit and the defer-Rollback pattern, and sqlx's extensions: named queries (:fieldname placeholders), StructScan and Select for mapping rows directly to structs. The interview question is always 'why use sqlx over an ORM?' — this module gives the production-grounded answer.

modules.title: GORM & Ent
modules.intro: GORM is the most popular ORM in the Go ecosystem, and Ent is the code-generation-based alternative gaining traction at larger companies. This module covers GORM's model conventions (gorm.Model with ID/CreatedAt/UpdatedAt/DeletedAt, soft deletes, naming conventions), association types (BelongsTo, HasMany, ManyToMany), the N+1 problem and how Preload and Joins fix it differently, GORM hooks (BeforeCreate, AfterUpdate — the trade-off between convenience and hidden behaviour), AutoMigrate vs manual migrations with goose or golang-migrate, and using db.Raw and db.Exec for queries GORM cannot express. Ent is covered from the design decision angle: schema-as-code with full type safety and codegen vs GORM's convention-over-configuration approach. The critical interview question is 'when would you drop to raw SQL instead of using an ORM?' — this module gives the honest answer.

modules.title: PostgreSQL with pgx
modules.intro: pgx is the high-performance, feature-complete PostgreSQL driver for Go, preferred over lib/pq for all new projects. This module covers pgx v5's API (pgxpool.New for connection pooling, pgx.Connect for single connections, the pgx.Row/pgx.Rows scanning API), pgx's native PostgreSQL type support (pgtype.Text, pgtype.UUID, pgtype.JSONB — avoiding the reflect-based scanning overhead of database/sql), the COPY protocol for bulk inserts (orders of magnitude faster than individual INSERTs for batch data loading), LISTEN/NOTIFY for lightweight pub/sub using an existing PostgreSQL connection, pgxpool configuration (MaxConns, MinConns, HealthCheckPeriod — how to tune for a FastAPI-style throughput pattern), and the production workflow: reading query plans with EXPLAIN ANALYZE from Go, catching missing indexes with pg_stat_user_indexes. The interview differentiator is understanding when pgx's low-level control justifies the complexity over GORM.

modules.title: Redis with Go
modules.intro: Redis with Go interview questions cover both the go-redis/v9 client and the patterns built on top of it for Go services. This module covers the go-redis v9 client (NewClient, NewClusterClient for Redis Cluster, connection pool configuration, context-aware commands), pipelining for batching commands in a single round trip, Lua scripting with Eval for atomic multi-key operations (the canonical use case: atomic rate limit counter increment + expiry), the Pub/Sub API (Subscribe, Receive, the goroutine-per-subscription pattern), Redis Streams as a lightweight Kafka alternative for Go services (XADD, XREADGROUP, consumer groups), implementing a distributed lock with SET NX EX and the Redlock algorithm trade-offs, and rate limiting with the token bucket pattern using a Lua script. The scenario question is always 'how would you implement a distributed rate limiter for a Go microservice using Redis?'

modules.title: REST API Design with Go
modules.intro: REST API design with Go interview questions test both your API design knowledge and your Go-specific implementation patterns. This module covers the RESTful resource model (URL design, HTTP verb semantics, idempotency, the 200/201/204/400/401/403/422/429 status code decisions in Go handlers), API versioning strategies (URL prefix /v1/, Accept header, query param — trade-offs for Go router configuration), cursor-based pagination (why offset pagination breaks on large Go + PostgreSQL tables), JWT authentication in Go (golang-jwt/jwt, the standard claims validation pattern, the algorithm confusion attack), middleware for rate limiting (token bucket with Redis, the X-RateLimit-* headers), automatic API documentation with swaggo (annotations → OpenAPI spec), and graceful shutdown with os.Signal, http.Server.Shutdown(ctx), and context cancellation. The scenario question interviewers love: 'your Go API is receiving duplicate POST requests — how do you make your handlers idempotent?'

modules.title: gRPC with Go
modules.intro: gRPC with Go is the most interview-tested protocol topic for Go backend roles — Go is the lingua franca of gRPC services, and almost every cloud-native company uses gRPC for internal service communication. This module covers the protobuf definition workflow (.proto file → protoc-gen-go → generated code), the four gRPC service types in Go (unary RPC for request/response, server streaming for paginated or event streams, client streaming for batch uploads, bidirectional streaming for realtime two-way communication), gRPC interceptors as Go's equivalent of HTTP middleware (UnaryInterceptor and StreamInterceptor), grpc.Dial with TLS, service discovery and load balancing with gRPC-Go, status codes and error propagation across service boundaries, and the gRPC vs REST comparison that comes up in every Go system design interview: when does the binary protocol, strong typing, and HTTP/2 multiplexing justify the protobuf toolchain overhead?

modules.title: Kafka & NATS with Go
modules.intro: Kafka and NATS are the two most common messaging systems in Go microservice architectures, each covering different needs. This module covers the confluent-kafka-go producer (delivery callbacks, async vs sync produce, error handling), the sarama consumer group (the most commonly used Kafka library in the Go community — ConsumeClaim, session.MarkMessage, rebalance handlers), offset management (manual commit, at-least-once vs exactly-once semantics in Go consumers), error handling patterns (dead-letter topics, the poison-pill consumer pattern), and the NATS messaging system — NATS core for at-most-once pub/sub (ideal for metrics, heartbeats, fire-and-forget), NATS JetStream for persistent, at-least-once messaging with consumer groups (the modern NATS persistence layer that competes with Kafka for simpler use cases). The interview comparison question: 'you need a message queue for your Go microservice — when do you pick NATS over Kafka?'

modules.title: GraphQL with Go (gqlgen)
modules.intro: GraphQL with Go using gqlgen is the idiomatic approach for Go GraphQL servers — schema-first code generation over runtime reflection. This module covers gqlgen's schema-first workflow (.graphql schema → generated Go types and resolver interfaces), writing resolver implementations (the generated Resolver struct, wiring to your service layer), the N+1 problem in GraphQL (a query for 100 users with their posts triggers 101 queries without dataloaders), the dataloader pattern (batching and caching per-request with graph-gophers/dataloader), GraphQL subscriptions over WebSockets in Go (the subscription resolver, concurrent writes to the subscription channel), and the architecture question every GraphQL interview asks: 'when would you choose GraphQL over REST?' and 'what are the security risks specific to GraphQL that you need to mitigate in a Go server?' (depth limiting, complexity analysis, introspection disabling in production).

modules.title: Design Patterns in Go
modules.intro: Design patterns in Go interview questions test whether you apply Go idioms or translate patterns from Java/Python without adaptation. This module covers the functional options pattern (the idiomatic Go alternative to the builder pattern and telescoping constructors — func WithTimeout(d time.Duration) Option), the middleware chain pattern (the http.Handler wrapping pattern that underpins every Go web framework), the repository pattern in Go (defining a storage interface, providing a PostgreSQL implementation, injecting a mock in tests), dependency injection without a framework (constructor injection using interfaces — Go favours small interfaces over DI containers), the observer pattern using channels (event streams without callbacks), and sync.Once as the Go singleton idiom. The SOLID principles are covered through Go examples: the 'I' in SOLID (interface segregation — why Go's small-interface philosophy is a direct expression of ISP) and the 'D' (dependency inversion — program to interfaces, not concrete types).

modules.title: Clean Architecture & Hexagonal in Go
modules.intro: Clean architecture in Go is a first-class interview topic at companies with large Go codebases — particularly when the interviewer asks 'how would you structure a Go microservice from scratch?'. This module covers the canonical four-layer Go service structure (handler → service → repository → model), hexagonal architecture (ports and adapters in Go — how to define a port as a Go interface, an adapter as a concrete struct implementing that interface, and how to swap implementations without touching business logic), dependency wiring with Google Wire and Uber fx (the build-tag-based approach vs the inject-at-runtime approach), event-driven architecture in Go (domain events as channel messages or Kafka events, the trade-off with synchronous service calls), and CQRS — command and query handlers as separate interfaces in Go. Every answer addresses the question interviewers ask before the pattern: 'how much architecture is the right amount for this codebase?'

modules.title: System Design Fundamentals
modules.intro: System design fundamentals questions are anchored to Go and cloud-native patterns. This module covers capacity estimation with Go service assumptions (a well-tuned Go HTTP server handles 10K–100K req/s on a single core; goroutine overhead at 2KB vs Java thread at 1MB), caching strategies anchored to Go services (go-redis cache-aside, in-memory LRU with golang-lru, the thundering herd problem and singleflight as the Go-idiomatic fix), horizontal scaling patterns for Go (stateless handlers + external state in Redis/Postgres, graceful shutdown with context propagation), the CAP theorem mapped to databases Go services commonly use (PostgreSQL = CP, Redis Cluster = AP-leaning, DynamoDB = tunable), consistent hashing for sharding (the jump hash algorithm used in Go distributed systems), and rate limiting design (token bucket in Go with Redis, the leaky bucket alternative). Examples throughout use Go-specific numbers and libraries.

modules.title: System Design Case Studies
modules.intro: System design case studies give you worked examples anchored to Go implementations. This module walks through five canonical problems: URL shortener (Go Gin + PostgreSQL for storage + Redis for redirect cache, the base62 encoding in Go), distributed rate limiter (Go middleware + Redis Lua script for atomic token bucket, deployed as a sidecar or middleware service), chat system (Go WebSocket server with gorilla/websocket + Redis pub/sub for horizontal scaling across multiple Go instances), distributed job queue (Go producer writing to a buffered channel or Redis stream + worker pool consuming it, graceful shutdown draining in-flight jobs), and API gateway in Go (reverse proxy with net/http/httputil, per-route rate limiting, JWT validation, service discovery integration). Each case study follows the standard system design format: requirements → capacity → API → data model → architecture → bottleneck deep-dive → trade-offs.

modules.title: Microservices with Go
modules.intro: Microservices with Go is a natural fit — Go's small binary size, fast startup, and built-in HTTP server make it the language of choice for Kubernetes-based microservice architectures. This module covers service decomposition principles applied to Go (bounded context → Go service, the monorepo vs multi-repo question for Go teams), service discovery (Consul, Kubernetes DNS, client-side vs server-side load balancing with gRPC), the circuit breaker pattern in Go (sony/gobreaker, the half-open state that distinguishes a circuit breaker from a retry loop), distributed tracing across Go services (OpenTelemetry SDK for Go — instrumented HTTP clients and gRPC interceptors, trace propagation via W3C Trace Context headers), the saga pattern for distributed transactions (choreography with Kafka vs orchestration with a Go state machine), and service mesh trade-offs (Istio/Envoy sidecar vs Go-native approaches). These questions come up at companies that have moved from a monolith to a Go microservices architecture.

modules.title: Application Security & OWASP in Go
modules.intro: Application security interview questions for Go cover both the OWASP top 10 as they manifest in Go services and Go-specific security pitfalls. This module covers SQL injection in Go (why parameterised queries via database/sql are safe, the anti-pattern of fmt.Sprintf in query strings), XSS (Go's html/template package auto-escapes; text/template does not — the wrong template choice is a production XSS vulnerability), JWT in Go (golang-jwt/jwt v5 — the algorithm confusion attack, alg:none, how to enforce HS256/RS256, the Parse vs ParseWithClaims distinction), OAuth2 in Go (golang.org/x/oauth2 client, the PKCE flow for native apps), TLS configuration (tls.Config in Go — cipher suites, minimum TLS version, certificate validation), secrets management (environment variables, AWS Secrets Manager via aws-sdk-go-v2, HashiCorp Vault with the Go client), and input validation (go-playground/validator tags, the sanitize-never-trust model for user input in Go APIs). Go's type system prevents certain vulnerability classes but not all.

modules.title: Testing in Go
modules.intro: Testing in Go is idiomatic and built into the language — no JUnit equivalent needed. This module covers the testing package (TestXxx naming convention, t.Error vs t.Fatal, t.Helper for test utility functions), table-driven tests (the idiomatic Go pattern for testing multiple cases — the slice-of-struct approach, when to use subtests vs parallel tests), testify's assert and require packages (assert continues on failure, require stops — the practical difference), t.Run for subtests (isolated scope, parallel subtests with t.Parallel()), benchmarks (BenchmarkXxx, b.ResetTimer, how to read benchmark output), TestMain for setup/teardown of shared test infrastructure (database connections, test containers), and the -race flag in tests to catch data races automatically. The interview question Go interviewers always ask: 'walk me through how you'd test a Go HTTP handler' — this module provides the complete answer.

modules.title: Mocking & Integration Testing
modules.intro: Mocking and integration testing in Go builds on the language's interface system — if you designed your dependencies as interfaces, mocking them is straightforward. This module covers gomock and mockgen (the code-generation-based mock library that generates type-safe mocks from your interfaces — EXPECT(), Return(), gomock.InOrder for sequential call assertions), manual interface mocking (writing a simple test-double struct that implements the interface — preferred for simpler cases), the httptest package (httptest.NewServer for spinning up a real HTTP server in tests, httptest.NewRecorder for testing handlers without a server), testcontainers-go (spinning up a real PostgreSQL container in a Go test, how to get the dynamic port, the module vs raw approach), golden file testing for testing JSON/protobuf response shapes, and the test pyramid applied to a Go microservice — how many unit tests, integration tests, and end-to-end tests are the right ratio and why.

modules.title: Docker for Go Applications
modules.intro: Docker for Go applications is a distinct topic from Docker in general — Go's single static binary changes the optimization strategy. This module covers the Go multi-stage Dockerfile (build stage with the full Go toolchain → final stage with only the compiled binary, achieving images under 20 MB), distroless and scratch base images (the trade-off: no shell, no package manager, but zero extra attack surface — and why Go's static binary makes this feasible while Python or Java cannot), CGO and the GOOS=linux GOARCH=amd64 CGO_ENABLED=0 flags for cross-compilation in CI, Docker Compose for the local Go development stack (Go service + PostgreSQL + Redis + Kafka), running as a non-root user in a Go container, health checks for a Go HTTP server using /healthz, and the scenario: 'your Go binary works locally but segfaults in the container — what are the first three things you check?'

modules.title: CI/CD for Go Projects
modules.intro: CI/CD for Go interview questions test whether you've shipped Go services to production, not just written Go code. This module covers a complete GitHub Actions pipeline for Go (go vet, staticcheck, golangci-lint, go test -race -coverprofile, build and push Docker image, deploy to Kubernetes), module caching in CI (caching $GOPATH/pkg/mod across runs — the difference between go.sum and go.mod for cache keys), golangci-lint as the standard Go linter aggregator (which linters matter: errcheck, gosec, staticcheck, gocritic), deployment strategies for Go services on Kubernetes (rolling update vs blue-green, the readiness probe requirements for zero-downtime deploys), Go binary versioning with ldflags (-X main.version=$(git describe --tags)), and the scenario questions: 'your Go test suite takes 8 minutes in CI — what are the first three things you'd optimise?' and 'a failing vet check is blocking release — how do you triage it?'

modules.title: Go Modules & Toolchain
modules.intro: Go modules are the standard for dependency management since Go 1.11, and the toolchain questions come up in every seniority-calibration round. This module covers the go.mod file (module path, Go version directive, require and indirect dependencies), go.sum (the cryptographic hash of every dependency version — why it's committed and what happens if it's missing), go get and go mod tidy (why tidy removes unused dependencies and how it affects go.sum), go work and multi-module workspaces (the Go 1.18+ feature for local development across multiple modules in a monorepo), replace directives (local replacement of a dependency — the pattern for forking a library, and why you must remove the replace before tagging a release), vendoring with go mod vendor (the trade-off between reproducibility and repository size), and go generate (the tool directive convention for running code generators — protoc, mockgen, sqlc, stringer). The interview question: 'how do you safely upgrade a transitive dependency in Go?'

modules.title: AWS with Go (aws-sdk-go-v2)
modules.intro: AWS with Go using the v2 SDK is the standard for Go cloud services. This module covers the aws-sdk-go-v2 configuration (config.LoadDefaultConfig, the credential chain — instance role > environment > shared credentials file, why you never hardcode keys), AWS Lambda with Go (the aws-lambda-go handler, the event types for API Gateway / S3 / SQS triggers, cold start optimisation for Go Lambdas — why Go's fast startup makes it excellent for Lambda), S3 operations (s3.Client, PutObject/GetObject, presigned URLs with s3.PresignClient, multipart upload for files over 5GB), DynamoDB (dynamodbattribute.MarshalMap, Query vs Scan, the expression builder for condition expressions), SQS (SendMessage, ReceiveMessage, DeleteMessage, the visibility timeout pattern for safe processing), IAM roles for service-to-service authentication (instance profiles, IRSA for Kubernetes), and ECS Fargate deployment patterns for Go services. The scenario: 'your Go Lambda is hitting the 15-minute timeout — what are your options?'

modules.title: Observability & Monitoring for Go
modules.intro: Observability for Go is a first-class interview topic at SRE-heavy companies. This module covers structured logging in Go (log/slog introduced in Go 1.21 — the standard library logger that finally does structured JSON output, slog.Logger, LogAttrs, the Handler interface), contextual logging (propagating a logger or trace ID through context.Context), OpenTelemetry SDK for Go (tracing with otel.Tracer, spans, attributes, the OTLP exporter — instrumenting a gin or net/http server, a gRPC client, a database query), the prometheus/client_golang library (Counter, Gauge, Histogram, Summary — the /metrics handler, custom metric registration, the four golden signals applied to a Go service), pprof in production (the net/http/pprof package, the go tool pprof flame graph, the expvar package for live Go metrics), and the scenario question that comes up at every SRE-leaning company: 'your Go service's p99 latency spiked — walk me through the investigation starting from your observability stack.'

modules.title: Production Operations & SRE for Go
modules.intro: Production operations and SRE interview questions for Go test whether you've run Go services under real traffic and real incidents. This module covers SLI/SLO/SLA applied to a Go HTTP service (defining the error budget from the SLO, how it drives deployment decisions), graceful shutdown in Go (signal.NotifyContext, http.Server.Shutdown with a deadline, draining in-flight requests and closing the database pool in the correct order), goroutine leak detection (the runtime.NumGoroutine metric, pprof goroutine profile, the patterns that cause leaks — goroutine blocked forever on a channel, goroutine waiting on a context that was never cancelled), memory leaks in Go (the difference between a GC pause and a genuine leak, how to detect a growing heap with pprof, the common causes: global maps that grow without bound, closures capturing large objects), Go-specific performance profiling (CPU flame graph with go tool pprof, allocation profiling with -memprofile, escape analysis with gcflags), and the incident response playbook for a Go service going down. These questions are asked at companies where Go is the primary service language.

modules.title: Behavioral & STAR for Go Engineers
modules.intro: Behavioral interview questions for Go engineers are the same questions every engineer faces, but the best answers are anchored to real Go projects, Go-specific trade-offs, and production incidents in Go services. This module covers the STAR format with the reflection beat (the meta-learning that separates rehearsed answers from self-aware ones), conflict resolution anchored to Go decisions (disagreement over using goroutines vs an external queue, interface design disputes, dependency selection debates like GORM vs sqlx), failure stories anchored to Go (the goroutine leak that took down a service, the data race that caused intermittent incorrect results, the context propagation bug that caused all requests to time out together), migration stories (moving from a monolith to Go microservices, introducing Go into a Python/Java team), and leadership moments (introducing the race detector and making it part of CI, mentoring a junior through their first concurrency bug, writing an ADR for a Go dependency choice). Every answer uses the reflection beat.

modules.title: Engineering Practices & Technical Leadership
modules.intro: Engineering practices interview questions filter for senior and staff Go engineers. This module covers code review for Go (what to flag first: exported types without comments, missing error checks, goroutine leaks, interface pollution — and how to give feedback that lands without the 'just use Java' subtext), technical debt strategy in Go (how to make the case for refactoring a 50k-line Go service, how to introduce golangci-lint incrementally without breaking the whole team), Architecture Decision Records for Go teams (when to write one — choosing between Gin and Echo, switching from database/sql to GORM, introducing generics into a pre-1.18 codebase), Go idiomatic code standards (gofmt is non-negotiable, effective Go naming conventions, the package-level documentation comment), and mentoring Go engineers (how to explain goroutine scheduling to someone who thinks in threads, how to introduce the context package to someone who's never used structured cancellation). Every answer uses the reflection beat — not 'here's what I did', but 'here's what I learned.'
